structures.name: Gerunds after like / love / hate / enjoy
forms: Subject + love/enjoy/like/don't mind/dislike/hate + verb-ing
I love swimming.
She enjoys reading books.
He hates getting up early.
We don't mind doing homework.
rules: After verbs of opinion (love, enjoy, like, don't mind, dislike, hate), use verb + -ing (gerund)
The gerund (-ing form) acts as a noun — it is the object of the opinion verb
Spelling: drop silent e before -ing (ride → riding); double consonant if short vowel + consonant (swim → swimming)
commonErrors: ❌ I love to swim. (incorrect for this structure — use -ing)
❌ She enjoy reading. (missing -s on enjoy for he/she/it)
❌ He hates get up early. (must use -ing after hate)
✅ He hates getting up early.

howOften.question: How often do you...?
howOften.example: How often do you go cycling? — I usually go cycling on Saturdays.

structures.examTips: Common error: using infinitive (to + verb) instead of gerund after like/love/enjoy/hate. Always use -ing.

structures.name: Comparative adjectives
forms: Short adjectives (1 syllable): adjective + -er + than
cold → colder than | hot → hotter than | big → bigger than
Long adjectives (2+ syllables): more + adjective + than
dangerous → more dangerous than | exciting → more exciting than
Irregular: good → better than | bad → worse than | far → further/farther than
as ... as: It is as cold as the North Pole.
rules: 1-syllable adjectives: add -er (short + single final consonant: double it — hot → hotter)
2-syllable adjectives ending in -y: change y to i + -er (foggy → foggier)
2+ syllable adjectives: use 'more' before the adjective
as...as: used for equal comparison; not as...as for unequal
commonErrors: ❌ It is more hot than yesterday.
✅ It is hotter than yesterday.
❌ London is more cold than Hanoi.
✅ London is colder than Hanoi.
❌ This storm is more bad than the last one.
✅ This storm is worse than the last one.
structures.examTips: Remember irregular comparatives: good→better, bad→worse. Never use 'more' with short adjectives like hot, cold, big, tall, fast.

structures.name: Present continuous (for now AND future arrangements)
structures.vietnameseName: Thì hiện tại tiếp diễn (hành động đang xảy ra và sắp xếp tương lai)
forms: Affirmative: Subject + am/is/are + verb-ing
Negative: Subject + am/is/are + not + verb-ing
Question: Am/Is/Are + Subject + verb-ing?
For future arrangements: I am meeting my friend tomorrow. (already planned)
rules: Use present continuous for: (1) actions happening right now; (2) fixed future arrangements
Spelling: drop silent e (make → making); double consonant if short vowel + consonant (run → running)
Key time words for future use: tomorrow, next week, on Saturday, this evening
commonErrors: ❌ I am liking pizza. (stative verb — 'like' is not used in continuous)
❌ She is go to school now.
✅ She is going to school now.
❌ They are travel to France next week.
✅ They are travelling to France next week.
structures.examTips: Stative verbs (like, love, know, want, have, need) are NOT normally used in continuous form. Also note: 'be going to' and 'present continuous for future' are different — present continuous implies a definite arrangement.

structures.name: be going to (future plans and intentions)
structures.vietnameseName: Cấu trúc be going to (kế hoạch và dự định tương lai)
forms: Affirmative: Subject + am/is/are + going to + verb
Negative: Subject + am/is/are + not + going to + verb
Question: Am/Is/Are + Subject + going to + verb?
I am going to buy new shoes tomorrow.
She isn't going to wear that dress.
Are you going to visit the market?
rules: Use 'going to' for plans already decided before speaking
Use 'going to' for predictions based on visible evidence
The verb after 'going to' is always the base form (infinitive without 'to')
commonErrors: ❌ I am going to bought shoes.
✅ I am going to buy shoes.
❌ She going to travel next week.
✅ She is going to travel next week.
❌ Are they going to to visit us?
✅ Are they going to visit us?
structures.examTips: Do not put 'to' after 'going to' again — the structure is 'going to + BASE verb', not 'going to + to + verb'. Also: 'going to go somewhere' is often replaced by 'going somewhere' in informal speech.

structures.name: Countable and uncountable nouns; some / any; How much / How many
structures.vietnameseName: Danh từ đếm được / không đếm được; some / any; How much / How many
forms: Countable: apple → apples | egg → eggs | banana → bananas
Uncountable: water, milk, rice, sugar, flour, butter, oil (NO plural -s)
some + affirmative: I need some sugar. / There are some apples.
any + question/negative: Is there any milk? / We don't have any flour.
How many + countable: How many eggs do we need?
How much + uncountable: How much water is left?
rules: Countable nouns can be singular or plural: one apple / two apples
Uncountable nouns have no plural form — never add -s
some → affirmative sentences; any → questions and negatives
Exception: use 'some' in questions when offering/requesting politely: 'Would you like some tea?'
How many → countable; How much → uncountable
commonErrors: ❌ I need some rices. (rice is uncountable)
✅ I need some rice.
❌ Are there some apples? (question → any)
✅ Are there any apples?
❌ How many milk do we have?
✅ How much milk do we have?
structures.examTips: The most tested point: remembering which nouns are uncountable (water, milk, rice, sugar, flour, butter, cheese, bread). Avoid adding -s to uncountable nouns.

structures.name: Past simple (regular and irregular verbs)
structures.vietnameseName: Thì quá khứ đơn (động từ có quy tắc và bất quy tắc)
forms: Regular affirmative: Subject + verb-ed
walked, played, visited, cooked, finished, watched
Irregular affirmative: go→went, come→came, see→saw, eat→ate, buy→bought, ride→rode, swim→swam, run→ran
Negative: Subject + didn't + base verb
She didn't come to school yesterday.
Question: Did + Subject + base verb?
Did you see that film? — Yes, I did. / No, I didn't.
rules: Regular verbs: add -ed (walk→walked; double consonant: stop→stopped; drop e: like→liked; y→ied: study→studied)
Irregular verbs must be memorised — there is no rule
For negatives and questions: use 'did' + BASE verb (NOT past form)
Time expressions: yesterday, last week, ago, in 2022
commonErrors: ❌ She didn't went to school. (use base verb after didn't)
✅ She didn't go to school.
❌ Did they ate lunch? (use base verb in questions)
✅ Did they eat lunch?
❌ We goed to the park. (go is irregular)
✅ We went to the park.
structures.examTips: Key irregular verbs to memorise: go/went, come/came, see/saw, eat/ate, have/had, buy/bought, run/ran, swim/swam, take/took, make/made, say/said, find/found.

structures.name: should / shouldn't (advice)
forms: Affirmative: Subject + should + base verb
You should rest and drink lots of water.
Negative: Subject + shouldn't + base verb
You shouldn't eat too much sugar.
Question: Should + Subject + base verb?
Should I see a doctor? — Yes, you should. / No, you shouldn't.
rules: should = it is a good idea to do this (advice / recommendation)
shouldn't = it is a bad idea to do this (negative advice)
The verb after should/shouldn't is always the BASE form
should is a modal verb — same form for all subjects (no -s for he/she/it)
commonErrors: ❌ You should to rest.
✅ You should rest.
❌ She shouldn't eats sweets.
✅ She shouldn't eat sweets.
❌ He shoulds go to the doctor.
✅ He should go to the doctor.
structures.examTips: No 'to' after should/shouldn't. No -s for he/she/it. Contrast: 'must' = obligation (stronger); 'should' = advice (softer, not compulsory).

structures.name: can / can't (present ability); could / couldn't (past ability)
structures.vietnameseName: Can/can't (khả năng hiện tại); could/couldn't (khả năng trong quá khứ)
forms: Present ability: Subject + can + base verb
I can swim. / She can't fly a plane.
Past ability: Subject + could + base verb
He could run very fast when he was young.
She couldn't speak English before she went to school.
Question (present): Can + Subject + base verb?
Can you ride a bike? — Yes, I can. / No, I can't.
Question (past): Could + Subject + base verb?
Could you cook when you were six?
rules: can/could are modal verbs — same form for all subjects
can → present ability or possibility
could → past ability (what you were able to do before)
The verb after can/can't/could/couldn't is always the BASE form
can also expresses permission and possibility: Can I open the window? / It can get very cold here.
commonErrors: ❌ She cans swim. (no -s on modal verbs)
✅ She can swim.
❌ They could to play the piano. (no 'to' after could)
✅ They could play the piano.
❌ I can't swam last year. (use could/couldn't for past)
✅ I couldn't swim last year.
structures.examTips: can = present; could = past. No -s for he/she/it. No 'to' after can/could. Contrast with 'be able to' which is more formal and works in all tenses.
